title: David Chen — Healthcare IT Procurement (Happy Path)
summary: David's experience leading the evaluation and procurement of a clinical decision support system. He navigates compliance complexity and stakeholder politics while trying to make a defensible, data-driven recommendation within a 6-month window.

actions: Receives notification from existing vendor of end-of-life date
Books initial planning meeting with CTO and clinical governance lead
laneContent.thoughts: Eighteen months to find, evaluate, and implement a replacement. That sounds like a lot until you factor in NHS procurement timelines. I need to start immediately.

actions: Facilitates three stakeholder workshops with clinical leads and operations
Translates clinical needs into technical and compliance requirements
Creates a requirements specification document for sign-off
laneContent.thoughts: The clinical leads know what they need operationally but they can't tell me whether they need HL7 FHIR or just a decent API. I have to translate between two different languages — clinical and technical — and also get this through legal. It's a juggling act.

barriers.description: Clinical director articulates needs in patient outcome terms; David has to infer the technical specification
barriers.emergesFrom: David's technical expertise clashes with clinical stakeholders' non-technical language — his precision frustrates him when he can't get the specification he needs to proceed safely

laneContent.needAtStep: A structured requirements template that prompts clinical stakeholders with the right questions — without requiring them to know what DSP Toolkit is
opportunities: Healthcare IT requirements canvas that bridges clinical needs and technical/compliance requirements
Pre-populated NHS compliance requirements to avoid stakeholders having to articulate what they can't know

actions: Issues RFI through Find a Tender Service
Searches G-Cloud for pre-approved vendors
Reviews Digital Health Intelligence market report
Sends direct outreach to 4 vendors with known NHS track records
laneContent.thoughts: There are a lot of vendors claiming NHS experience that have done one pilot in a 50-bed community trust. I need to separate genuine NHS-at-scale providers from the ones who've rebranded their generic SaaS with a stock photo of a hospital.

barriers.description: Vendor marketing claims are hard to verify without reference calls — market scan produces a list, not a quality signal
barriers.emergesFrom: David's risk-averse, data-driven approach is undermined by a market where genuine NHS credentials are hard to distinguish from aspirational marketing

laneContent.needAtStep: An independent NHS IT vendor registry that shows verified reference sites, DSP compliance status, and implementation track record — not vendor self-reporting

actions: Scores 12 RFI responses against weighted criteria matrix
Presents shortlist of 4 vendors to internal panel
Secures sign-off from CTO and clinical governance lead
laneContent.thoughts: The scoring is only as good as the criteria. I've weighted compliance at 35%, clinical fit at 30%, commercial at 20%, implementation track record at 15%. But the CTO will want to talk about integration architecture. I need to have that conversation now, not at demo stage.

actions: Schedules 4 vendor demonstrations over 3 weeks
Distributes demo evaluation scorecard to panel (6 evaluators)
Sends structured question set to vendors 48 hours before each demo
Attends one reference site visit for the leading vendor
laneContent.thoughts: I sent them the compliance question set in advance. Half of them are still hand-waving on DSP. One vendor actually came with a pre-completed evidence pack — that tells me something about how they'll handle implementation. The others are telling me what I want to hear.

barriers.description: Vendors avoid specific answers on DSP Toolkit coverage — it requires persistent follow-up questions that slow the demo flow
barriers.emergesFrom: David's precision and compliance focus collides with vendors who have learned to deflect hard questions — his frustration peaks when technical evasion is dressed up as flexibility

laneContent.painAtStep: Having to chase vendors for DSP evidence packs after the demo. The evaluation scorecard is now blocked on compliance questions, and the clinical panel is impatient to make a decision.

momentThatMatters.description: One vendor provides a pre-completed DSP evidence pack unprompted — this signals genuine NHS readiness and shifts David's assessment decisively

actions: Briefs preferred vendor on DSP Toolkit evidence requirements
Coordinates DPO review of Data Processing Agreement
Commissions penetration test from approved third-party supplier
laneContent.thoughts: Our DPO is shared with two other trusts. She has a three-week queue. The vendor's evidence pack is incomplete — they're missing the business continuity element. I can't submit to the DPO until this is resolved. The timeline is slipping.

barriers.description: Shared DPO creates a bottleneck — David cannot control the audit timeline
barriers.emergesFrom: David's methodical risk management is blocked by organisational resource constraints entirely outside his control — the tension between his professional standards and his capacity to deliver on time is acute

laneContent.needAtStep: A clear checklist of what a complete DSP evidence submission looks like — ideally one the vendor can self-certify against before submission, so the DPO review isn't the first quality check
opportunities: Vendor DSP pre-submission checklist to shift quality left
Shared NHS DPO capacity model or specialist DPO service for smaller trusts

actions: Receives DPO sign-off with two minor conditions
Agrees remediation plan with vendor for outstanding items
Documents decision in procurement log
laneContent.thoughts: Conditional approval with two action items. The vendor accepted both conditions without pushback. That's the right signal — a compliant vendor takes compliance seriously. We can proceed.

actions: Contacts three NHS organisations known to use the vendor (two from vendor references, one via NHS CIO Network)
Conducts structured 45-minute reference calls focused on implementation, support, and post-go-live compliance
laneContent.thoughts: The vendor gave me two glowing references. I found a third independently through the CIO network — the one they didn't give me. That conversation was more useful than the other two combined. The onboarding took 40% longer than contracted, but support was responsive when things went wrong.
laneContent.needAtStep: A way to surface independent peer references from NHS colleagues who've used the vendor — not just the vendor's preferred advocates
opportunities: NHS Digital Health vendor review platform (peer-rated, verified by trust affiliation)

actions: Builds ROI model: time savings, compliance risk reduction, avoided incident costs
Writes five-case business case following HM Treasury model
Reviews draft with CFO before board submission
laneContent.thoughts: The CFO wants to see the ROI in year two, not year five. But the real value — reduced compliance risk, avoided clinical incidents, better data for QI — doesn't sit neatly in a spreadsheet. I need to present both: the financial case and the risk case. The CFO will approve the financial case; the CEO will approve the risk case.

barriers.description: Quantifying compliance risk reduction in financial terms requires assumptions the CFO may not accept
barriers.emergesFrom: David's technical and compliance expertise is fully visible to him but opaque to the board — he must translate complex risk into financial language without oversimplifying to the point of inaccuracy

laneContent.painAtStep: The five-case model template is structured for infrastructure projects. Applying it to a SaaS procurement with complex compliance implications requires significant interpretation — there's no healthcare IT-specific guidance.

actions: Presents business case to Executive Committee
Answers CFO questions on TCO and exit provisions
Responds to CEO question on clinical benefit evidence
laneContent.thoughts: The CFO is focused on the exit clause. The CEO wants to hear from the clinical lead, not me. I've prepared a clinical benefits summary from the clinical governance lead for exactly this question. The board wants to be reassured, not impressed.
laneContent.needAtStep: A one-page clinical benefit summary that a clinical governance lead — not an IT Director — can present convincingly to a non-technical board

momentThatMatters.description: The clinical director speaks compellingly about patient safety implications — this shifts the board from cautious to convinced

actions: Receives unanimous board approval
Notifies vendor and procurement team
laneContent.thoughts: Six months of work, and it comes down to a 40-minute board meeting. But the groundwork was right. When the CFO asked about exit provisions, I had the answer. When the CEO asked about clinical benefit, the clinical director had the answer. Preparation made this look easy.

actions: Passes approved business case to procurement and legal teams
Monitors contract review progress against procurement timeline
Escalates two significant redlines to CTO for decision
laneContent.thoughts: Legal is taking longer than I'd like. The vendor has redlined our standard exit provision — they want 12 months notice for contract termination, we want 6. This is a legitimate business risk. I've escalated to the CTO. We can't let legal drag us past the implementation window.

barriers.description: Vendor legal team responds slowly to redlines — multiple rounds of review are adding 3-4 weeks to contract closure
barriers.emergesFrom: David's drive to execute conflicts with the necessarily slow pace of legal review — he knows every week of delay is a week of implementation risk

laneContent.painAtStep: There's no clear escalation path when vendor legal response times are causing timeline risk. The procurement team can't force the vendor's lawyers.

actions: Signs project charter with vendor
Establishes project governance structure: steering group, working group, clinical champions
Registers project with PMO and confirms delivery milestones
laneContent.thoughts: Contract signed. Implementation lead from the vendor is excellent — she's done three NHS deployments and knows the DSP audit cycle. That reference from the CIO network paid off — I knew what to ask for in the implementation team.

momentThatMatters.description: Vendor implementation lead briefs the team with an NHS-specific deployment plan — David recognises genuine NHS expertise immediately

actions: Documents lessons learned
Closes procurement process in PMO system
Briefs CTO on implementation risks and mitigation plan
laneContent.thoughts: Twenty weeks. Within the window. The compliance process was slower than planned but the outcome is solid. The vendor we chose is the right one — not the cheapest, not the flashiest demo, but the one that took compliance seriously from day one. That matters in healthcare.

outcome.reflection: A methodical, evidence-based procurement process that prioritised compliance without sacrificing clinical fit. The 20-week timeline was tight but achievable. The key insight: the vendor who takes compliance seriously in procurement will take it seriously in implementation.
learnings: Independent reference discovery via peer networks is more valuable than vendor-provided references
A pre-completed DSP evidence pack from a vendor is a leading indicator of implementation quality
Clinical director involvement in the board presentation was decisive — IT Directors should not present clinical benefit alone

researchSources.source: NHS IT procurement process research and David Chen actor development
